prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

After Cai Guo-Qiang Quick, before the sun rises, get up one more time, my grandmother. The artist won’t mind if you borrow his sky ladder. Place your foot on the bottom rung and keep climbing, even though you’re a skeleton with a broken neck from falling downstairs on Guy Fawkes night. The ladder is wrapped in gunpowder, and he’s lit the touchpaper. Your bones are ascending firecrackers. You’re half a kilometer high now, halfway to the universe, my joy-gardener. I hope you find a garden with rich black soil for your black roses, hybrids like you— half white half Indian, half woman half flower, their roots twined through your skull, you who were transplanted among the pale roses of a British family. Your skin now a mix of photons and soot. What do you find up there? Is there a hothouse? Are there alien hands with deft brushes pollinating stars? Remember how your tomatoes kept yielding more planets? Are there constellations of exotic fruit now you’ve reached the top? Have you gone back enough in space-time to when you were alive? The ladder is charred, the hot air balloon that held it up is about to collapse. The explosions are over. Cai showers his head with champagne, as his 100-year-old granny watches on her cell phone.Did you see it? He asks,did you hear the whoosh, the rat-tat-tat at the starry door? You can go back to sleep now

*After Cai Guo-Qiang*

Quick, before the sun rises, rise one more time, my grandmother. The artist will not mind if you borrow his sky ladder. Set your foot upon the lowest rung and keep climbing—even though you are a skeleton, your neck broken in a fall down the stairs on Guy Fawkes night. The ladder is wrapped in gunpowder, and he has lit the touchpaper. Your bones are ascending firecrackers now.

You are half a kilometer high, halfway to the universe, my gardener of joy. I hope you find a garden of rich black soil for your black roses—hybrids, like you: half white, half Indian; half woman, half flower, their roots entwined through your skull. You who were transplanted among the pale roses of a British family, your skin now an alloy of photons and soot.

What do you find up there? Is there a hothouse? Are there alien hands with deft brushes, pollinating the stars? Do you remember how your tomatoes kept yielding more planets? Are there constellations of exotic fruit, now that you have reached the summit? Have you traveled far enough back through space and time to arrive at the moment when you were alive?

The ladder is charred; the hot-air balloon that held it aloft is beginning to collapse. The explosions are over. Cai showers his head with champagne, while his hundred-year-old grandmother watches on her cell phone.

Did you see it? he asks. Did you hear the whoosh, the rat-tat-tat at the starry door?

You can go back to sleep now.

Set your foot on the lowest rung and keep going upward, even as a skeleton whose neck snapped in a tumble down the stairs on Guy Fawkes night. Gunpowder coats the ladder, and the touchpaper is already burning. Your bones become rising fireworks. Already you've climbed half a kilometer, my joy-gardener, halfway toward the cosmos. May you discover a garden there with fertile dark earth suited to your black roses—hybrids, just as you were, half white and half Indian, half woman and half blossom, their roots wound through your skull, you who were replanted among the fair roses of an English family. Now your skin blends light particles with soot. What awaits you above? Might there be a greenhouse? Could alien fingers wield delicate brushes to pollinate the stars? Do you recall the way your tomatoes kept producing more worlds? Now that you've climbed to the summit, are there clusters of strange fruit shaped like constellations? Have you traveled far enough through space and time to reach the days when you still lived? The ladder is now blackened, and the hot air balloon suspending it is on the verge of giving way. The blasts have ceased. Cai pours champagne over his own head while his 100-year-old grandmother watches through her phone. Did you catch it? he wonders aloud—did you hear the rush of air, the rat-tat-tat against heaven's door? Rest now; you may return to sleep.

# Climbing Toward the Universe

In this evocative poem, the speaker addresses their deceased grandmother directly, urging her to borrow the artist Cai Guo-Qiang's "sky ladder"—a spectacular installation wrapped in gunpowder that, when ignited, burns a fiery pathway ascending into the heavens. With this striking image, the speaker invites their grandmother to climb toward the universe, transforming her death into a luminous departure rather than a final end.

The grandmother is portrayed with unflinching physicality as a skeleton, her body reduced to bare bones. We learn that she died from a broken neck after falling down the stairs on Guy Fawkes Night—a poignant and cruelly ironic detail, given that this British celebration is marked by bonfires and exploding fireworks. The gunpowder of Cai Guo-Qiang's ladder thus echoes the very night of her death, binding tragedy and celebration together in a single, glowing image.

Beyond mourning, the poem becomes a celebration of the grandmother's mixed heritage. She is described as half white and half Indian, a hybrid figure likened to a "black rose"—a rare and beautiful bloom transplanted among the pale roses of a British family. This botanical metaphor honors her difference and singularity, acknowledging the way she stood apart, distinctive and vivid, within a family and a country that did not share her origins.

Drawing on this imagery of flowers and cultivation, the speaker imagines a celestial garden waiting for the grandmother at the summit of her ascent. There, she might discover rich soil, hothouses, and constellations of exotic fruit—a heavenly landscape that reflects and rewards her earthly love of gardening. In this vision, the afterlife is not a void but a flourishing paradise perfectly suited to her passions, where she can finally tend and belong.

The piece concludes by turning to Cai Guo-Qiang himself, who celebrates the successful realization of his sky ladder artwork while his own hundred-year-old grandmother watches the event on her phone. This closing image draws a tender parallel between the artist's tribute to his living grandmother and the speaker's tribute to their deceased one. In both cases, a grandson and a granddaughter reach toward the sky in acts of love, art, and remembrance—uniting the personal and the cosmic in a shared gesture of devotion.

# The Sky Ladder: An Elegy in Fire

At the heart of this poem lies a striking act of transformation, in which the artist Cai Guo-Qiang's celebrated "Sky Ladder"—a ladder of gunpowder set alight to burn a fiery path into the night sky—becomes the vehicle for an intimate address to a grandmother who has died. Rather than mourning in conventional terms, the speaker reimagines the moment of loss as a spectacular ascent, envisioning the grandmother's skeletal form climbing rung by rung through a series of gunpowder explosions. Each burst of light and heat propels her further from the earth, until she moves toward a celestial garden waiting at the ladder's uppermost reaches. In this way, the physics of the artwork—its brief, violent, luminous life—supplies the poem with a language capable of holding both catastrophe and beauty in the same breath.

Threaded through this central image is a meditation on the complexities of mixed-race identity. The speaker occupies the space between Indian and British heritage, and the grandmother stands as a figure who embodies questions of belonging, inheritance, and displacement. The poem is preoccupied with what it means to be transplanted—to be rooted in one soil while flowering in another—and it treats the grandmother's death as a kind of final relocation, a passage between worlds that echoes the migrations and cultural crossings that have shaped the family's history. Her upward journey becomes not only a departure from life but a negotiation of the many homes, real and imagined, that a person carries within them.

The imagery sustains this double vision of grief and wonder with remarkable tenderness. Black roses bloom throughout the poem, at once funereal and strange, suggesting mourning that refuses to be ordinary. A cosmic garden opens overhead, offering a destination that is lush, expansive, and otherworldly, a place where the transplanted self might finally take root. Most memorably, the grandmother's bones are rendered as firecrackers—fragile, combustible, and capable of dazzling release—so that her body itself becomes part of the artwork's incandescent display. These images allow the poem to convert the rawness of loss and the ache of cultural dislocation into something luminous, treating transcendence not as an escape from pain but as its transfiguration.

By the poem's close, the spectacle has run its course, and the fire has done its work. Having carried the grandmother upward through explosion and light, the poem grants her the rest she has earned, settling her at last within the celestial garden. What begins in the language of detonation ends in the language of peace, and the reader is left with the sense that grief, however violent its passage, can resolve into stillness. In transforming a deceased grandmother's memory into a figure who climbs the sky, the poem offers a moving vision of how the displaced and the mourned might finally arrive somewhere they belong.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem addressed to a dead grandmother, inspired by Cai Guo-Qiang's "Sky Ladder" gunpowder artwork, using her mixed British-Indian heritage and imagery of gardening, roses, and firecrackers.
counterfactuals.output:
# Sky Ladder

Grandmother, they lit a ladder in the sky once—half a kilometre of fire climbing into the dark over a fishing village, and I thought of you, how you were always half here and half elsewhere, one foot in the rose beds of Sussex, one in the marigold heat you never named aloud.

You planted like an apology. The English roses first—*Gertrude Jekyll*, *Constance Spry*—their names like women you'd wanted to become, pruned back hard each autumn, disciplined into blooming. But at the far end of the garden, where the fence gave way to wildness, you let the other things grow. Jasmine that climbed without permission. Something orange and unruly you touched but would not explain.

I never asked the right questions. That is the grief of it.

When the artist raised his ladder of gunpowder, the whole thing burned upward in seconds—a staircase made of the very thing that destroys staircases. He built it for his own grandmother, you know. She was a hundred, watching on a small screen, too frail to stand beneath the sky she'd given him. I understand now why a man would spend twenty years learning to write his love in explosions. Some tenderness is too large for the tongue. It needs the whole horizon.

You came from firecracker countries, Grandmother—both of them, if you count the ration and the raj, the way empire is its own long fuse. Diwali and Bonfire Night, Guy Fawkes and Lakshmi, all that burning to keep the dark back. You never told me which fires were celebration and which were memory of things lost. Perhaps you no longer knew. Perhaps that is what it means to be made of two places: every light doubles, every spark falls two ways.

I want to say the ladder reached you. That somewhere above the roses and the unnamed orange flowers, a rung of fire touched the hem of wherever you've gone.

But I am my grandmother's child, and I know the truth of gardens: everything blooms by being cut. Everything climbs by burning. The ladder does not last. It flares, it writes its impossible sentence against the night, and then there is only smoke drifting east over the water, and the ordinary stars, and a boy—a girl, a whole family of us—standing in the ash-fall, faces tipped up, saying *thank you* to someone who cannot hear, in a language she half-taught us, in the half-light she left behind.

The roses are still yours. I prune them wrong.

The jasmine has taken the whole fence now. I let it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental elegy for my grandmother who died falling downstairs on Guy Fawkes night. She was half Indian, half white, and loved gardening. Use Cai Guo-Qiang's sky ladder as the central image.
counterfactuals.output:
**Sky Ladder, for Nani**
*(Cai Guo-Qiang, Quanzhou, 2015 — 500 metres of fire, one dawn)*

---

He tied it to a balloon. He lit the bottom rung.

She came down the other way.

—

Guy Fawkes, and the sky already
committing arson over the terraces,
each garden throwing up its own brief scaffold of light—

                    and you,
                    between the seventh stair and the sixth,
                    learning the physics
                    of the wrong direction.

—

*Rung.* A word for the past tense of ringing.
The bell of you, gone quiet in the hall.

—

Here is the ladder he built. Read it upward:

              sky
              the       into
                    fire   of
              structure  a
              standing,      briefly
              gunpowder,  and    fuse
              rope,   ash,
              scaffold,
              net,
              hemp,
              rope,
              earth—

Two hundred years of your two bloods
climbing in smoke: Bengal to Birmingham,
marigold to marigold,
the same orange you planted at both ends of the world
without ever calling it the same flower.

—

You gardened like someone who trusted descent:
seed *down*, root *down*, the whole faith of it downward
and the reward arriving later, up,
where you weren't looking.

So maybe the stairs were only planting.
Maybe you went into the dark of the house
the way you pushed a bulb into November soil,

              certain
              of what
              spring
              owed you.

—

Cai's ladder burned for two and a half minutes.
Long enough for his grandmother, a hundred, nearly blind,
to see it from her bed. He made it *for* her.
Fire climbing away from a woman
who could no longer climb.

I make you this one.
Lie back. I've lit the balloon.

—

The neighbours think it's fireworks.
Let them. Let the whole street
mistake your leaving for celebration,
your name for a rocket's *ohh*,
the smoke of you for weather.

—

              Not fallen.
                    Released.
              Not down.
                    Only the first rung
                    of a longer stairs,
                    the ones that go the way
                    gunpowder goes—

              up,
              up,
              up into the ordinary Guy Fawkes dark

              until even the ash
              turns and drifts back down
              to settle, warm, on the marigolds,

              which is to say: on you,
              which is to say: on you again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem titled "After Cai Guo-Qiang" that imagines a skeleton grandmother ascending his sky ladder toward the universe, weaving in themes of transplantation, race, gardens, and fireworks.
counterfactuals.output:
# After Cai Guo-Qiang

She climbs the ladder made of gunpowder and light,
her bones a scaffolding of borrowed calcium,
each rung a flare that blooms then dies against the night—
a grandmother of ash, ascending toward the sum

of all she carried in the steerage of her chest:
a fistful of seeds sewn into a coat's torn lining,
the memory of soil she pressed but never quite possessed,
transplanted twice, and rooted in the act of climbing.

They said her kind would never grow in this cold ground.
They measured her in shades, in almond of the eye,
in syllables they could not shape without a wound.
She answered them by learning how to occupy

the sky. Her ribs are trellises where jasmine used to run.
Her skull a lantern hollowed for a paper moon.
The garden she abandoned blossoms overhead—
each firework a chrysanthemum that opens up too soon

and scatters. This is how the dead migrate: as spark,
as the brief cartography of embers over water,
as gunpowder unspooling script across the dark
in a language only ancestors and children after

can read. She does not look back down the fuse.
The ladder burns behind her, rung by falling rung.
What is a race but seed that someone chose to lose
then found again, replanted, flowering among

the constellations? Grandmother, keep climbing.
The universe is one enormous open plot
where every exiled root is given room, in time,
to bloom in colors this small earth forgot—

and when the last flare gutters, when the smoke unwinds,
we'll find her handprint pressed in soot against the stars:
proof that the transplanted travel farther than their minds,
that ash remembers gardens, and that we are ours.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output:
# The Ladder of Light

You would have loved this—
how the man from Quanzhou tethered fire to the sky,
a ladder of gunpowder climbing five hundred meters
into the throat of dawn,
each rung a struck match against the dark.

*Cai Guo-Qiang did this for his grandmother,*
I whisper to the space where you used to be,
her hundredth year celebrated in sparks
that opened like chrysanthemums
against the indifferent blue.

---

Grandmother, I have been learning the botany of absence.

How grief is a seed that does not ask permission,
how it roots in the chambers of the heart
and blooms at inconvenient hours—
2 a.m., the grocery store, the smell of jasmine
that was your perfume, your kitchen, your hands.

I keep finding you in the peripheries:
the way light bends through a water glass,
the champagne bubbles rising
like small souls ascending,
each one carrying a fragment of what we couldn't say.

---

They lit the ladder and the whole sky became
a garden burning upward,
petals of flame unfolding into smoke,
into memory, into the particular ache
of watching something beautiful
that cannot last.

This is what I've learned about the cosmos:
we are all made of collapsed stars,
you and I,
the same carbon that composes diamonds
and the graphite of the pencils
you used to write your recipes,
your letters, your name.

---

So when I raise this glass—
its golden effervescence, its small celebration—
I am toasting the ladder and the ash it becomes,
the way endings are also a kind of flowering.

You are the space between the rungs now,
the dark that makes the fire visible,
the soil from which this strange bloom of missing you
grows and grows and grows.

The ladder burns.
The champagne rises.
And somewhere in the great orchard of the sky,
you are tending stars,
gathering their light into your apron
like the tomatoes you grew,
like everything you ever loved
and let go
and loved again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
